item.title: Resources
item.description: Seattle University thankfully already offers some resources for those who face challenges with food. But I feel that the resources should be advertised more. We currently have the food pantry, where students can get free groceries, but the process requires you to fill out an application, which some can feel embarrassing. There is also the case that some students may only need temporary help, and filling out a full application can feel arduous. There is the food recovery program, which makes ready to eat meals available, but those are only available at certain locations like the military/veteran link, or the commuter link. I think this program could be enhanced to provide greater access to ready-to-eat meals for the student population. One way to do this is to have the same program run out of The Cave at Campion Hall. This would allow students facing food insecurity to go to a place they are comfortable with, to get a ready-to-eat meal when they need it. Resources

item.title: about page
item.description: My name is Matthew Beavers, and I am a sophomore at Seattle University. I was inspired to create this project because I have Celiac disease and am also allergic to cow milk. This project was designed for Seattle University students. I was also inspired to create this project because of the book Revolutions a Very Short Introduction by Goldstone. I read this book for my UCOR 3400 class, and while reading it I noticed that there were two elements of revolution from the book that could be applied to this project. The first is fiscal strains, given that we are college students and during a time when the economy due to the current United States administration is suffering. (Goldstone, 2023) The second is “increasingly widespread popular anger at injustice.” (Goldstone, 2023) Many feel like they are being scammed with the dining experience at Seattle University, and the more time I spend at this university, the more I notice how upset people are with dining. So I have taken it upon myself to try to be an advocate for Seattle University students, and while I cannot speak for everyone, I will do my best to keep everyone’s best interests at heart.

item.title: Moving Forward
item.description: So, how do we address change? There are a couple of different options that Seattle University could take. One study from a California school found that students express “a desire for practical financial and food literacy “life skills’ training” (Watson, et al. 2016) Given the Jesuit nature of our university, with the value of cura personalis, Seattle University could offer a training on food literacy during orientation. This could include budgeting, where to find food resources on campus like the ready-to-eat meals, and perhaps an expediated application for the food pantry at the training as well. Like I say in the resources section, there could also be free ready-to-eat meals at The Cave. Some other alternative solutions could be decreasing the overall cost of the food and increasing hours. I know that would be very difficult, given the current state of the economy and prices of food, but given the high tuiton costs for the school, many students including myself feel like we are being taken advantaged of due to the required on campus housing and meal plan for freshmen and sophomores. Even more so when the precieved value for cost of the food is low. As for increasing hours, most students spend their breaks on campus, so dining should be prepared for that, and not close all but two locations that run for limited hours on the breaks. For people who have jobs, these inconsistent hours make it near impossible to eat on campus during breaks, and often have to go else where and spend extra money on food when they shouldn’t have to. There is the counter point that students should be able to prepare meals for themselves, many students have difficulty accessing a kitchen, and may not have the proper supplies, and when they go to borrow supplies they are typically unavailable or extremely limited. One of the students I interviewed said that when they borrowed kitchen supplies, they recieved a singular saucepan and nothing else, which is hardly adequate to properly cook with.

item.title: Personal Experience
item.description: As someone with food allergies, my dining experience at Seattle University has been severely limited because of them. There is only one place on campus I can consistently eat at, which is Thrive Without Nine. But there are multiple problems with Thrive Without Nine. There have been consistent problems with it, mainly the pricing and the portion sizes. The price per calorie at Thrive is much higher when compared to other campus spots such as Fusion or the Bistro, and on average they give less calories. The small portion sizes/lack of calories have directly caused me to lose weight this year, and I’ve dropped approximately 10lbs since starting in the fall. Whenever I go to eat on campus, it feels like my hands are tied and I am forced to eat at Thrive. Whenever I try to eat anywhere else I run the risk of getting cross contaminated, which has serious dehabilitating effects on my health and academic performance. I have already repeated gotten sick, causing me to miss class and even quizzes. This has caused me to personally lose faith in Seattle University’s dining, because it is hard not to feel scammed every meal, and hard to trust that the food provided is actually safe for people with sensitive allergies like me.

item.title: Student Testimonials
item.description:
One of the reasons why I wanted to advocate for this topic is because many of my peers have had issues with the current dining experience at Seattle University. So, I decided to interview a few of my peers on what issues they have with the dining experience, and what they want to change.

Common themes were items are overpriced, and should be priced better. There should be better hours, especically on weekends/holidays. For students who are out of state and cannot go home for breaks, it feels like there is very little access to food during said breaks. There were also overall complaints of lack of variety for students who eat on campus all year, and have done for multiple years. The average score out of 10 for dining was a 5.5.
